The 2023 Analytical Report found no body responsible for enforcing the right to free movement of workers; Law No. 200/2025 gives the Equality Council that competence and the role of national contact point, as the Government reports in a machine-translated source, and the 2026 report confirms that the law entered into force in March 2026 to align with the acquis on workers' free movement rights. The improvement is legal only: the 2026 report does not assess the body, and no item among the 15 Moldova items on this issue shows it at work.

Law No. 200/2025 is adopted and designates the Equality Council, which answers the 2023 finding in law. The amendment of the Equality Council law, the Council's restructuring and extra staff, training for public authority and Council staff, and information measures by the General Inspectorate for Migration are all still planned, and the Council had filled 19 of 33 posts (Government figures, machine translated). What remains is a body that in practice supports EU workers and informs them of their rights, with the mandate, structure and staff to do so.

The missing enforcement body is raised only in the 2023 Analytical Report; a search of all Moldova EU items for the Equality Council or an enforcement body found no later mention, and no benchmark, Reform Agenda payment condition or key recommendation names it. It is a specific acquis obligation within the chapter but not central to it, and the 2026 key recommendations address alignment and equal treatment of EU workers in general terms.

The legal designation is done, and the remaining steps (amending the Equality Council law, restructuring and recruiting) are within the Government's control, with one lead body already in place. Staffing is the main constraint: the Council had 19 of 33 planned posts filled and its anti-discrimination directorate 4 of 7 (Government figures, machine translated).

Sub-area wording on the European Health Insurance Card, which matches this issue, records no progress in 2025, and the finding that no national health insurance card exists because there is no integrated health information system is unchanged in the 2023 report, the 2023 Analytical Report and the 2024 and 2025 reports. In 2026 the Commission reports a finalised feasibility study and an approved EHIC Action Plan, which are planning steps and do not yet show a change in the card or the health information system.

The 2025 and 2026 key recommendations still require IT infrastructure, systems and capacity for the EHIC scheme. Only the feasibility study is implemented: the EHIC module in the health insurance information system, the amendments to the health care and health insurance laws, the technical specifications of the card and the integrated health information system are planned or under development, and the Government states that the EU acts on the card are not yet transposed (machine translated). What remains is a national health insurance card and the IT, legal and administrative basis to issue and accept the European Health Insurance Card at accession.

The EHIC is named in the Chapter 2 key recommendations of 2025 and 2026, and the finding that its domestic preconditions are missing is repeated in each report from 2023 to 2025, with no progress recorded in 2025. Issuing and accepting the card is a core acquis requirement for accession, which is why the issue is rated High although the key recommendation itself appears in only two reports.

The national health insurance company coordinates the work, the feasibility study is finished, an action plan sets a roadmap and the law amendments are planned for 2026. Against that, the card depends on an integrated health information system that the Commission found missing in each report from 2023 to 2025, and the insurer's IT directorate had 3 of 8 planned specialists (machine translated).

Consulting the authority and acting on its opinions is a procedural step within the control of the Government and Parliament, and the authority already reviews a large number of drafts. No item shows past progress or resistance on the uptake of its advice, so the rating rests on the nature of the mechanism alone.

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this issue concerns only part of Chapter 23. The 2024 report says justice digitalisation needs to improve, the 2025 report that the new Agency for Digitalisation in Justice needs faster operationalisation, and the 2026 report finds the Agency's capacity extremely limited and the use of IT tools across the justice system uneven and partial. The August 2026 amendments promoting digitalisation of some judicial procedures are recorded but not yet assessed.

The 2026 report calls for further legal improvements and a decisive strengthening of the Agency, and a 2026 key recommendation asks for substantial progress on an integrated electronic case management system for law enforcement and prosecution bodies. The Agency exists but has extremely limited capacity, the August 2026 amendments are adopted, and the E-File application, which the Reform Agenda requires in all first instance courts by December 2027, is still planned. What remains is digital communication with courts in practice and connected IT across justice institutions, run by an agency able to deliver it.

Digital case filing in courts is a Reform Agenda payment condition (E-File in all first instance courts by December 2027), an integrated case management system for law enforcement and prosecution is a 2026 key recommendation, and justice digitalisation is raised in each report from 2024 to 2026. All EU items on this issue are flagged as of doubtful fit with the technology theme; if the case management elements are treated as back-office court IT outside scope, this would be Medium.

Progress needs courts, prosecution and law enforcement bodies to adopt connected systems, and the agency set up to deliver this has extremely limited capacity because of persistent staffing problems in 2026. Past progress is limited to setting up the agency in 2025 and the August 2026 amendments, and IT use remains uneven.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter: some level of preparation from 2023 to 2025 and moderately prepared in 2026. The 2026 report finds that the new legal framework reinforced the regulator's administrative and financial independence, and the Commission's 2026 release decision records access tariffs for the incumbent's infrastructure cut by 16% to 49% from 1 March 2026, against minimal network sharing (0.95%) in the 2025 baseline. The gain on independence is legal only, and an ITU finding reported in the Government's 2025 programme still describes independence and accountability as insufficient (machine translated).

The Reform Agenda requires at least 3% of the incumbent's infrastructure to be shared and network-sharing agreements by the incumbent; access tariffs have been cut and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act transposed in June 2026, but the agreements are still planned and none of the 51 Moldova items on this issue reports the sharing rate after the 0.95% baseline. The law reinforcing the regulator's independence is adopted, and the regulator had filled 105 of 114 posts by March 2026. What remains is independence shown in practice and competitive safeguards that actually raise infrastructure sharing in a market where the incumbent holds more than half of broadband.

The Reform Agenda conditions on infrastructure sharing touch the competition side of this issue, but they are framed as implementing the Electronic Communications Code and the Gigabit Infrastructure Act, whose alignment belongs to the legal alignment issue. Regulator independence is not named in any benchmark or key recommendation among the 51 Moldova items on this issue; if the sharing conditions are read as central to this issue, this would be High.

The levers are legal and regulatory and within national control, and recent delivery is strong: a new law in force from January 2026, updated access tariffs in force within the Reform Agenda timetable, working arrangements with BEREC from 2025 and a regulator close to full staffing. The main constraint is market concentration, with the incumbent holding more than half of broadband.

The Chapter 6 scale is context only, since this is part of the chapter. The 2023 report and the 2023 Analytical Report found company law not aligned on digital tools and processes, the 2024 report repeated the recommendation while recording a qualified electronic signature for filing with the business register, and the 2026 report records the new State Register of Legal Entities, launched in December 2025, which enables registration of all legal forms. The Government's own assessment (machine translated) is that the directive on digital tools in company law is only partly transposed.

The latest EU requirement, from 2024, is further alignment on the use of digital tools and processes in company law. Electronic signature filing and the new register are implemented, but the draft law on digital tools in company law is still planned, online company registration ran by e-mail as a provisional solution, and in February 2026 the new platform offered online only name reservation and register extracts (machine translated). What remains is full transposition of the rules on digital tools and processes, with company formation and filings fully online through the new register.

Digital tools in company law appear in the 2023 recommendation and among many elements of the 2024 key recommendation on company law, but in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition among the 29 Moldova items on this issue, and no 2025 or 2026 item among them repeats the recommendation. It is a defined acquis requirement but a narrow part of Chapter 6; the Reform Agenda step on the new register is counted under the base registers issue.

The remaining work is mainly legal and within the Government's control, a draft law is prepared, and the new register is in place. Its development slipped from a planned July 2025 launch to December 2025, and such delays are the main risk (Government figures, machine translated).

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is a cross-cutting data protection issue. Breaches are confirmed every year (105 in 2022 in the 2023 report, 173 in 2024 in CSO Meter and 173 in 2025 in the authority's machine-translated report), the 2025 report records a major health data breach, and the authority reports in 2026 that state bodies still access personal data through the COI technology. Rising complaints are read by CSO Meter as growing awareness rather than worse compliance, so they are not used as a trend.

The 2023 requirement to train public servants and raise awareness has been answered by the authority's 2025 training campaign of 84 courses for over 3,600 people, and Law No. 195/2024, adopted and in force from 23 August 2026, lets the authority impose administrative sanctions directly (machine translated). Sources conflict on data access: the Government says data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, while the authority finds state bodies still using the COI technology outside it, and only about 50 public authorities had designated a data protection officer. What remains is compliance in practice by public and private controllers, including in health, with the new sanctions applied and access to state registers made traceable.

Data protection compliance is raised in the 2023 recommendation on training and awareness and in the 2025 key recommendation on health, which names the protection of personal data, but in no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition among the 62 Moldova items on this issue, and not across three or more reports. Applying data protection law is central to the data theme, but the volume of authority and civil society material does not raise priority.

The new law gives the authority direct administrative sanctions, ending the duplicated procedures it blames for weak deterrence, and courts upheld its measures in 52 of 58 final cases in 2025. Against that, compliance depends on many public and private controllers, and the authority reports years of unanswered requests to move state bodies off the COI technology (machine translated).

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this is a cross-cutting e-government issue. The Commission found the civil service human resources information system not functional in 2023 and 2024, its replacement only in incipient design in 2025 and still in development in 2026. Shared platforms such as MCloud, MPass, MPay and MConnect were already in place before the period, as the Reform Agenda notes, so they show no change.

Most shared building blocks are implemented and in use, but the human resources management system, which the Reform Agenda requires with at least three modules by December 2027, is still in development, the permits system was used fully or partly by only 16 of 31 issuing institutions at the 2024 audit, and the eArhiva system is planned. Sources conflict on the register of state information systems: SIGMA says all resources and systems were registered, while the Court of Accounts finds registration delayed. What remains is a working human resources management system and consistent use of shared systems by all institutions, including those not subordinate to the Government.

The human resources management system is a Reform Agenda payment condition and is reported in each year from 2023 to 2026, but these items are flagged as of doubtful fit with the technology theme because the system mainly serves civil service management, and the Commission otherwise records the shared platforms as in place. If the system is treated as a core e-government building block, this would be High.

Moldova has a long record of building shared platforms through the e-Governance Agency, and the human resources system has a Reform Agenda deadline. Against that, the earlier system failed through problems with its private provider, its replacement has moved slowly since 2023, and institutions not subordinate to the Government declined to use the permits system (machine translated).

The chapter scale was not decisive, since this issue spans several chapters; the 2026 Chapter 6 rating of some progress cites the new register and is context only. The Commission recorded the business register's paper archive digitalised by August 2024 and the State Register of Legal Units launched on 29 December 2025, a Reform Agenda step it judged satisfactorily fulfilled, while the public property register was in progress in 2025 and still pending in 2026. The State Population Register concept was withdrawn in August 2025 and resumed in 2026 (machine translated), so not every register moved.

The 2025 and 2026 key recommendations require completing the digitalisation of the public property register, which remains in progress, and the Reform Agenda requires a digital cadastre covering 98% of the territory by December 2027; the legal entities register is implemented. Sources conflict on the register of state information systems: SIGMA says all were registered, while the Court of Accounts finds registration delayed and 63% of registered systems not properly documented. What remains is a fully digital public property register, the planned modernisation of the population register and the cadastre, and reliable data across base registers.

Base registers are named in two Reform Agenda payment conditions (the State Register of Legal Units and the digital cadastre), and the public property register is a key recommendation in 2025 and 2026; reliable base registers are central to the data and digital government themes. The legal entities register condition is already met, so the rating rests mainly on the cadastre condition and the repeated recommendation.

The legal entities register was delivered with World Bank support, about six months after its planned July 2025 launch, and the civil status records system went into production in November 2025. Against that, the population register concept was suspended in 2025, the public property register has been in progress since 2025, and the Commission found the Public Services Agency short of administrative capacity in 2024.

The Chapter 10 scale is context only, though its progress wording in 2024 and 2025 cites the digitalisation of public services. Commission figures rise in each report: about 40% of business services online in 2023, about 40% of mapped services in 2024, over 50% in 2025 (64% for businesses and 54% for individuals in 2024), and in 2026 70.3% of the 636 services on the EVO portal online, 82% of business and 61% of citizen services digitalised and user uptake up significantly. Government counts of 2023 business service requests conflict between its 2024 and 2025 documents, so they are not used for the trend.

The Reform Agenda target of 75% of business services digitalised has been met, and EVO, the public services portal and 118 Unified Public Service Centres are in use; but in 2026 only 61% of citizen services are digitalised, only 133 of 414 business services run fully end to end, the Reform Agenda notes that the portal lacks integration with EU systems, and the link to the Single Digital Gateway is still planned. Demand remains low in rural areas, which is why the Commission says the centres were set up. What remains is a fuller range of citizen services delivered end to end online, integration with EU systems, and use by people with weaker digital access or skills.

Digital public services are the subject of Reform Agenda payment conditions (75% of business services digitalised, met in 2026, and the EVO Sign wallet extended to at least 20 services), and the Commission cites them in its Chapter 10 progress wording in 2024 and 2025; the portal and its services are central to the digital government theme. The large volume of Government and survey material did not count towards priority.

Progress has been steady and measured by the Commission in every report from 2023 to 2026, the e-Governance Agency runs the shared platforms, and the work is tied to Reform Agenda funding. The main constraints are cost, which the Government says exceeds its own resources, and low demand among older and rural users.
